#2687. Dolphins vs. Colts final score, immediate reactions: Kyle McCord plays well as special teams fail Miami

The Miami Dolphins faced the Indianapolis Colts in Week 10, with starting quarterback Kyle McCord in his NFL debut after an injury to Malik Willis. A game featuring two teams in contention for the first-overall pick in the 2027 NFL Draft, it felt like that at times. Neither team executed a complete game, but in the end, the Colts held on to squeak out the win.

The Dolphins fell to 1-8 with the loss to the Colts. They had chances to win this game, but they lost after three kicks failed to put points on the board. The game was put on the shoulders of a young quarterback, and he responded. The offense moved the ball well enough to win the game. The defense shut down the Colts' offense, especially in the second half. The Dolphins should be walking out of Indianapolis with a win.

In the end, the special teams failed Miami.

In the long run, this game could prove important to the Dolphins as they look toward the 2027 NFL Draft. Miami falling to 1-8 keeps them in contention for the first-overall pick and pushes the Colts further away from claiming it. Even better, the Colts' pick is owned by the New York Jets after a trade last year. Not allowing an AFC East division rival to jump them in the draft order could be a way to find a silver lining on an ugly black cloud of a day.

I'm trying to find the positive in what should have been a Miami win but now goes down as yet another loss.

Washington had himself a day. The highlight will be his 34-yard touchdown pass to Jalen Tolbert on a double-pass play, but he was all over the offense on Sunday. He had three catches for 50 yards, plus returned four punts for 36 yards.

Brooks was a wrecking ball throughout the game. He was just everywhere – in the backfield, shutting down runs at the line of scrimmage, breaking up passes in coverage. He was a force throughout the game. He led the game with nine tackles, had a pass defensed, and a forced fumble. It was a great day for Miami's All-Pro linebacker.

Miami's offense is built to run the ball, and Gordon was not afraid to take carry after carry, despite the Colts stacking the box and daring Miami to find a way to run. Gordon had to grind out some of his runs, but in the end he tallied 20 carries for 76 yards along with four receptions for 39 yards.

McCord spent his entire rookie season on the Philadelphia Eagles' practice squad, then joined the Green Bay Packers for training camp this year. Miami traded for him at the end of the preseason, and he made his NFL debut in this game as the starting quarterback. The game never felt too big for McCord. Some plays looked like a young player trying to force something, but overall, McCord was solid all game and kept the Dolphins in the game. He finished the game 17-for-32 for 209 yards and a 73.6 passer rating. He also ran twice for four yards and a touchdown.

Note: "Losers" is not a judgment on the talent or character of any individual. It is simply a categorization of the play in one game – no disrespect is intended or should be inferred

I think there is a rule that someone from the special teams unit has to appear in the losers list this year. Gonzalez lands here after missing a 47-yard field goal attempt in the first quarter. Miami's defense is playing hard to take some of the stress off a quarterback making his first career start. The offense did enough to move the ball down into Colts territory. Gonzalez just booted the ball left. He responded in the second half with a 53-yard field goal, but then missed an extra point and another field goal later in the game. Miami has to have better from their kicking game. Miami lost this game by two points. Gonzalez missed seven points' worth of kicks.

It seems like every time Wright is in the backfield and takes a handoff, he gets hit almost immediately. The same isn't true of Gordon's rushing attempts. It might be confirmation bias, and there is space on some of his runs, but it really does seem that Wright just cannot buy the space he needs to even try to make a move or get up to speed.

Miami opened the second half with the ball. On the kickoff return, safety Julius Wood was called for an illegal block, backing Miami up to their own 15-yard line. On Miami's first play, cornerback Justin Walley's blitz got to McCord's blindside, stripped him as he tried to throw, and the Colts fell on the ball in the end zone. Miami had a chance to answer the Colts and tied up the game to open the half, but everything went wrong, and suddenly the Dolphins were down two touchdowns.

The Dolphins are a team still working through their growth and development as a rebuilding team. That is true in every aspect of the game, but that is no excuse for some of the issues on special teams. Even if some tackling issues or lane assignments are due to younger players, the miscues in the kicking game are inexcusable. I know I already listed Gonzalez above, but this is more about the unit as a whole. The Dolphins cannot afford to give up big gains, get flagged for holding or illegal blocks on returns, or miss kicks that take points off the board. Miami has to fix special teams, now.

#2685. Emotional Kirk Cousins: "It's been a tough three years. There's more to the story being written."

Three years ago, quarterback Kirk Cousins played the last game of his first stint with the Vikings at Lambeau Field, tearing an Achilles tendon during a Week 8 game. The first game of his second stint happened on Sunday.

The Vikings won, 30-10, completing the season sweep of the Packers and moving to 7-2 on the season. And Cousins was visibility emotional during his an-field interview after the win with Lindsey Thiry of ESPN.

He also made good decisions in key moments, helping the Vikings’ offense convert eight of 15 third-down situations.

It all happened after Cousins showed up only four days before the game. He now has a full week to prepare for a game against the 49ers — the last team he plated during his nine-game run in Las Vegas.

#2679. Belgium vs Italy: The tactics board - Mark van Bommel’s high-frequency transitions overwhelm the Azzurri

Belgium secured a dominant 4-1 victory over Italy by exploiting space in transition and clinical creative output from Charles De Ketelaere. Despite an early lead for the visitors, Mark van Bommel's tactical setup systematically dismantled Italy's defensive structure.

The tactical narrative of this UEFA Nations League clash was defined by a contrast in control versus chaos. Van Bommel entered the match with a clear mandate: to weaponise Belgium's explosive wide talent and use high-turnover situations to bypass Italy's technical midfield. While Italy sought to dictate the tempo through superior ball possession, Belgium's strategy focused on verticality and rapid counter-attacks, looking to exploit the space left behind by the aggressive Italian full-backs.

Roberto Mancini, conversely, aimed to utilise a fluid 4-3-3 system that morphed into a 3-2-5 in possession, prioritising ball retention to stifle the Brussels crowd. The tactical objective for the Azzurri was to isolate Pio Esposito against the Belgian central defenders while using Nicolo Barella and Sandro Tonali to create numerical superiorities in the half-spaces. However, this commitment to an expansive attacking shape eventually became their undoing as Belgium's structure proved more resilient under pressure.

Van Bommel deployed a 4-2-3-1 formation that functioned with immense tactical discipline. The defensive block remained compact, usually sitting in a mid-press that only triggered when Italy's Nicolo Fagioli or Alessandro Bastoni attempted to carry the ball across the halfway line. The double pivot of Youri Tielemans and Romeo Lavia was essential, providing a screen that forced Italy to play wide, where Belgium felt comfortable engaging in 1v1 duels. When possession was regained, the trigger was immediate: find Kevin De Bruyne or De Ketelaere to launch vertical transitions.

The role of De Ketelaere was particularly nuanced; he operated as a roaming playmaker, drifting between the lines to provide two crucial assists. By dragging Italian defenders out of position, he created the space for Maxim De Cuyper to arrive late for the equaliser in the 15th minute. Belgium's attacking patterns frequently involved overloads on the right flank before switching rapidly to Jeremy Doku on the left. This "switch of play" tactic exploited Michael Kayode's high starting position, eventually allowing Doku to score the third goal in the 26th minute after a relentless period of Belgian pressure that saw them score three times in just eleven minutes.

Italy initiated the match in a 4-3-3 that looked highly effective in the opening ten minutes. Their build-up play focused on short, triangular passing sequences between Kayode, Barella, and Esposito. This paid immediate dividends in the 11th minute when Kayode's delivery found Esposito for the opening goal. Defensively, Mancini employed a high line, intending to squeeze the pitch and limit De Bruyne's time on the ball, but this left them vulnerable to the pace of Diego Moreira and Doku.

The primary issue for Italy was the lack of defensive cover in the transition phase. When Fagioli and Niccolo Pisilli pushed forward to support the attack, the gap between the midfield and the back four became a chasm. Even with Bastoni and Riccardo Calafiori's ball-playing ability, they struggled when Belgium forced long balls into the channels. Italy finished with more possession (53%), yet their xG of 2.273 compared to Belgium's 3.355 suggests that while they had the ball, they lacked the defensive stability to manage the quality of chances they were conceding on the break.

The defining tactical battle took place in the central corridor between Belgium's double pivot and Italy's interior midfielders. Van Bommel won this battle by instructing his wingers to tuck inside when out of possession, creating a central block of six players that Italy simply could not play through. This forced the Azzurri to rely on crosses - completing 23 over the course of the match - which Brandon Mechele and Nathan Ngoy dealt with effectively. The mismatch was evident: Italy wanted a game of patience, while Belgium forced a game of sprints.

Mancini's decision to maintain a high defensive line even after conceding the equaliser was the turning point. By not dropping the block to account for Belgium's speed, Italy allowed Doku and De Ketelaere to dictate the tempo of the counter-attacks. The 2-1 goal by Ngoy in the 22nd minute, coming so shortly after the equaliser, psychologically broke Italy's tactical composure, leading to a frantic ten-minute spell where their defensive shape completely evaporated.

Trailing 3-1 at the break, Mancini attempted to rectify the midfield imbalance by introducing Federico Dimarco and Issa Doumbia for Fagioli and Pisilli. The move to a more traditional wing-back system was designed to provide better width and defensive tracking. Initially, this steadied the ship, as Italy saw more of the ball in the second half, but they lacked the clinical edge to convert their 12 total shots into goals. The yellow card for Tonali shortly before his 62nd-minute substitution highlighted the frustration of a midfield that was being bypassed too easily.

Van Bommel responded with pragmatic substitutions to see the game out. Bringing on Nicolas Raskin for Lavia added fresh energy to the press, while the introduction of Dodi Lukebakio and Leandro Trossard in the final minutes maintained the threat on the break. The most significant late adjustment was the instruction for Moreira to sit slightly deeper before exploding forward; this paid off in the 80th minute when he latched onto a De Bruyne pass to make it 4-1, effectively ending any Italian hopes of a comeback. Belgium's ability to maintain their intensity through substitutions was superior to Italy's structural changes.

Ultimately, Belgium's victory was a triumph of transitional efficiency over possession-based aesthetics. Van Bommel's decision to concede the ball and strike rapidly through the creative hubs of De Bruyne and De Ketelaere exposed Italy's high defensive line and slow central recovery. While Italy's early goal suggested a different outcome, their inability to adjust their defensive height in response to Belgium's pace led to the three-goal blitz in the first half. Belgium's superior shot quality and clinical finishing in big moments ensured a comprehensive tactical victory in Brussels.

#2674. KC Current upsets No. 1-seeded Gotham in NWSL semifinal, setting up Final appearance vs. Spirit

The Kansas City Current are heading to the NWSL Final after getting revenge on Gotham FC, with a 2-1 upset on the road on Sunday.

One year after Gotham stunned the Current with a 2-1 win in the quarterfinals, ending a historic NWSL Shield run, Kansas City flipped the script. Gotham entered the game as the No. 1 seed and the reigning champions, but will fall short of a back-to-back attempt thanks to a late goal from Haley Hopkins.

In front of a small 5,000-person crowd at New York City's Icahn Stadium — selected after concerns over the quality of the field at Gotham's typical home venue — Kansas City took the lead in the 20th minute after a beautiful direct free kick from Croix Bethune. In physics-defying fashion, the 25-year-old midfielder curved the ball around the Gotham wall and buried it into the lower left corner.

For the second week in a row, Gotham failed to hit a single shot on target — but still managed to get a goal. This week, though, it wasn't enough.

Still, even with Gotham's offensive struggles continuing, the team was able to get on the board in the 69th minute, after Midge Purce's cross forced an own goal. It was the second week in a row, after the team's 1-0 win over the Seattle Reign in the quarterfinals, where Gotham's only points came off an own goal.

As time began to run out, Current captain Lo'eau Labonta nearly pulled her team ahead by hitting a strike that bounced off the right post. Meanwhile, Gotham keeper Ann-Katrin Berger, one of the finalists for NWSL Goalkeeper of the Year, continued her stunning run with a number of miraculous saves.

But in the 89th minute, Haley Hopkins hit a strike off a set piece that hit the crossbar, going down and in to send Kansas City to the championship.

After lifting the Shield a few weeks ago, Gotham is denied the double in what has become a trend in the NWSL. Only three of the league's Shield winners have gone on to win the Final, as the league's balance has led to a number of high-profile upsets over the years.

The Current will now face the Washington Spirit, who secured their third straight spot in the Final after a 2-1 comeback win over the Utah Royals. Kessler, in his first year with the Lakers, also brings size and defense, supplying 10.8 RPG and 2.2 BPG, while sitting second in the NBA in dunks this season, with 42. Fellow big man Sandro Mamukelashvili has impressed as of late, scoring 23 points in each of the Lakers' last two games.

On the other side of the ledger, the Suns have won four of five, with the sole loss in that span coming at the hands of the aforementioned San Antonio Spurs. Over those five games, Devin Booker has averaged 26.6 PPG, 5.4 APG, and 2.0 SPG, and is starting to round into the form that Suns fans are used to seeing from their superstar over the last decade.

Quentin Grimes — AVAILABLE (Right Finger)

Austin Reaves — OUT (Left Heel Contusion)

Collin Sexton — QUESTIONABLE (Right Orbital Laceration)

Adou Thiero — QUESTIONABLE (Left Ankle Sprain)

The Lakers boast the NBA's best offense, with an offensive rating of 122.7. The Suns, on the other hand, have a defensive rating of 117.6, which ranks 26th in the NBA. If the Suns want a shot at pulling off the upset and not allowing the Lakers to extend their winning streak to eight, their bottom-tier defense will need to slow the Lakers' top-tier offense.

Austin Reaves being out should, in theory, help. But the Lakers managed fine in the one game this season that they were without Reaves, a 124-114 win over the Atlanta Hawks. In that game, Collin Sexton (18 points and 6 assists) and Mamukelashvili (23 points and 8 rebounds) picked up the slack, and did so while shooting a combined 8-12 from three. Sexton is also questionable for this game, so his presence (or lack thereof) would remove another weapon from the Lakers' potent offense.

Consistent with their respective offensive and defensive efforts this season, the Lakers also come to town as the NBA's third-best three-point shooting team this season, shooting a combined 38.3%. Conversely, the Suns have allowed opponents to shoot 37.4% from three this season, good for 25th in the league. Even without Reaves and (possibly) Sexton, the Lakers can still shoot the ball, and the Suns will need to find a way to stop them.

While the Lakers' offense has been spectacular, one area where they — like the Suns — struggle is in rebounding. Despite the size of Kessler and Mamukelashvili, the Lakers find themselves 27th in the NBA in rebounds per game. The Suns, unfortunately, find themselves dead last in that category. But coming off a game where the Charlotte Hornets out-rebounded them by 21, welcoming a subpar rebounding team to town could be a recipe for some rebounding success.

Lastly, we cannot ignore the fact that Devin Booker and Luka Doncic will be taking the same court. Whenever that happens, there is always a good chance of some extra entertainment. Two superstars with a penchant for gamesmanship and trash talk are always a recipe for entertainment.

Don't let Walker Kessler do to them what Wendell Carter, Jr., and Donovan Clingan did to them: 27/13 and 24/11, respectively. Kessler is a big dude, and surprisingly athletic for his size. The Suns have struggled against bigs like him this season, and if those struggles continue, they could be in for a long afternoon. Luka is going to get his, but with Reaves out, the Suns cannot let Kessler go off.

On the other side of the ball, someone needs to help Devin Booker. Book has been fantastic, but the rest of the starters have been hit or miss. While the Lakers' offense has impressed, its defense is middling. If the Suns want to win this game, they cannot afford to have starters not named Devin Booker combine to shoot 13-33, as they did against the Hornets.

This one stays close throughout. Book and Luka put on a show down the stretch, going shot for shot and jab for jab. In the end, the Suns pull out the upset.

#2670. Patrick Mahomes makes Chiefs' new pieces fit in needed win vs. Falcons | Opinion

With Kenneth Walker III missing and Travis Kelce knocked out of the game briefly, Patrick Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs were pressed to create some new ways to roll inside Mercedes-Benz Stadium on Sunday. And fast.

Mahomes was undoubtedly looking for you as he pulled out a vintage performance, so to speak, just when his team needed it.

Johnson, the fourth-round rookie backup for Walker, filled in with plenty of pop as Kansas City – fueled by Mahomes' season-high five touchdown passes – blew out the Atlanta Falcons 35-13 to claim first place again (on a tiebreaker) in the AFC West.

With Walker, who ranks second in the NFL with 872 rushing yards this season, nursing a groin injury, Johnson marked his first NFL start by leading the Chiefs with 163 yards from scrimmage and scoring two touchdowns. He rushed for 93 yards and caught six passes for 70 yards, including the 12-yard catch-and-dart job to the end zone to cap KC's first drive.

Downs, a fourth-year pro, was not to be totally overshadowed after arriving to Kansas City just before the NFL trade deadline struck on Tuesday. The fourth-year receiver (four catches, 53 yards) instantly made his presence felt as the reliable target Mahomes sorely needs.

He marked the occasion with an 18-yard TD catch off a pretty back-shoulder throw by Mahomes that said something about how quickly timing and rhythm can be achieved. Suddenly in the middle of a playoff chase, it was another reason, too, why Downs has no qualms about getting traded from the sinking Indianapolis Colts.

Then there was Cyrus Allen. The rookie receiver posted his first NFL touchdown on a go route in the third quarter, when Mahomes hit him with a perfect strike.

The Chiefs (7-2) really need this about now, after losing two of their past three games to put a damper on their 5-0 start. And with the injuries piling up – all-pro guard Trey Smith was knocked out the game with a concussion and tight end Jared Wiley was ruled out early with an ankle injury – the Chiefs couldn't afford a slip-up against the underachieving-yet-still-dangerous Falcons.

Kelce's ankle injury, suffered as he snagged a 23-yard catch on KC's second offensive snap, had the look of a bad omen. Yet that turned out as temporary. After fear was fueled by the sight of Kelce gingerly walking to the locker room for further evaluation, the star tight end returned later in the first half, providing reason for Mahomes and Chiefs Kingdom to exhale.

Then again, there may be more reasons for the Chiefs to hold their breath coming just around the corner. After a matchup next Sunday against the Cardinals, the Chiefs will engage in a brutal stretch of three consecutive road games – at Buffalo, at the Los Angeles Rams, at Cincinnati – that figures to weigh heavily on whether Andy Reid's team makes it back to the playoffs this season.

So, the Chiefs surely could use the type of low-stress victory that presented itself on Sunday.

Even better, Mahomes bounced back from the elbow injury suffered a week earlier in the victory against the Jets. He threw for 348 yards and five TDs (22-for-35), didn't have an interception and ran twice for 15 yards. In other words, all systems were a go.

In garbage time, the prolific quarterback connected with Andrew Armstrong for a 43-yard touchdown on a throw that was, well, classic Mahomes. He rolled right, pumped, scanned and lofted. Armstrong adjusted to high-point the pass at the goal line. Touchdown.

Armstrong who? The former Arkansas receiver entered the league as an undrafted free agent in 2025. And yes, it was his first touchdown, too.

Turns out it was quite the coming out party for the Chiefs. They discovered some new ways to support their magician of a quarterback, a few more elements to help win.

Now if they can keep all of that flowing.

#2666. Walker Kessler’s defensive impact goes far beyond the box score

When the Lakers initially traded for Walker Kessler, the on-court fit was easy to envision. One of the best shot blockers and rebounders in basketball, paired with the league's highest-scoring duo.

He's been as advertised. Kessler leads the team in blocks, rebounds, and double-doubles, but his impact goes beyond the traditional box score.

While the team is just 18th in defense, lineups with him next to Luka Dončić and Austin Reaves are a +26.6 net, with a 104.2 defensive rating so far, which would rank second overall league-wide. He's played and started every game for the 11-2 Lakers, who've won seven straight.

His main value comes from protecting the basket from all types of attacks. He's the anchor of the team's defense and gives the perimeter players the freedom to play more aggressively with him behind them.

His reputation as a rim protector showed itself instantly. Even when he doesn't get a block, Kessler's presence in the paint alters shots in the restricted area or prevents them from occurring at all.

Watch below as Milwaukee's athletic big man Kel'el Ware tries to attack him head-on from the top of the key. He drives right into the massive 7'2" frame, uses a pump fake and sees daylight, but leaves the shot short out of fear of his shot-blocking ability.

Verticality and contesting without fouling are two must-haves for any defensive center in the modern NBA. Kessler pairs both with excellent timing and instincts around the rim. The Lakers are switching on the perimeter in the clip below, which can be susceptible to straight-line drives when not communicated correctly.

Watch as Matisse Thybulle is late ball-watching and recovering to his switch, allowing his man an open driving lane.

Kessler jumps with two hands and puts the player in an impossible situation. There's no window for a shot or pass, and he's forced to throw it to the corner where it's picked off.

"They do show up in the stats. It's not box score stats," head coach JJ Redick said at practice Saturday. "We shared this with the group the other day, just to give a sense of how valuable he is to our defense. … Going into yesterday's game, Walker was second in the league, and only a point behind Wemby [in rim points saved]. Talking about one of the best rim protectors in the NBA. That doesn't always show up in blocked shots and steals. He's doing a fantastic job for us."

Rim protection is normally the final result of the defended action, but Kessler is involved in multiple plays throughout a possession..

Notice in the clip below how the Bucks attempt to run two ball screen actions. One is a regular pick and roll, while the other is a double drag with two screeners. Kessler is in his traditional drop coverage on both.

The ball never falls below the 3-point line, and the Bucks are forced into a late-clock heave that doesn't hit iron. It turns into another stop going the other way.

The mark of a good defensive big man is how many efforts they can make on a given possession. In the clip below, the Bucks get multiple drives to the rim, with Kessler there to not only protect the rim but also recover and get into the right help positions after a kick-out pass. After three different attacks, it ends in a shot clock violation.

He gets almost nothing in the box score from the possessions shown above, but the Lakers get a stop on all of them. The Lakers signed Kessler to a four-year, $130M deal in the offseason. With his contract locked up, his role couldn't be clearer.

Even if the traditional stats don't immediately scream out his value, the Lakers' defensive numbers do. And most importantly, so do the wins.

#2663. Observations after Sixers beat Bucks to move to 3-0, Embiid posts triple-double

Observations after Sixers beat Bucks to move to 3-0, Embiid posts triple-double originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers stayed unbeaten Saturday night at Xfinity Mobile Arena, earning a 127-116 win over the Bucks and improving to 3-0 on the season.

Joel Embiid had his 10th career regular-season triple-double, tallying 28 points, 11 rebounds and 10 assists.

On his 30th birthday, Jaylen Brown posted 27 points and five assists. Tyrese Maxey had 26 points. VJ Edgecombe scored 17 and grabbed 13 boards.

The Sixers' absences on the first night of a back-to-back included LeBron James (low back/sciatica management). Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said pregame that he did not know yet who would be available for his team's matchup with the Pistons on Sunday.

Here are observations on the Sixers' victory Saturday:

Dean Wade made his Sixers debut and started in James' place. He'd missed the first two games of the regular season with a left ankle sprain.

The 3-and-D forward scored the night's first points by a sinking a corner three-pointer on the opening possession.

Embiid also had a sharp start. He moved well, made good decisions and served as the main hub of his team's offense in the early going.

The Sixers' seven-time All-Star center has often enjoyed facing Myles Turner. He entered the night with an average of 29.4 points in 18 previous games against the Bucks big man.

Embiid did a little bit of everything in the first quarter, posting eight points, four assists and four rebounds over nine minutes. After snatching an offensive board, Embiid drained a fadeaway jumper to give the Sixers a 10-1 lead.

One of Embiid's assists was quite stylish. He found Edgecombe open beyond the arc with a behind-the-back bounce pass. Edgecombe knocked down the shot and wound up going 3 for 4 from three-point range in the first quarter.

The Sixers added rookie Labaron Philon Jr. to their rotation. Jabari Walker stayed in the mix, though he didn't enter until the 7:36 mark of the second quarter.

Philon played four minutes in his NBA debut and missed his lone shot attempt, a corner three. On defense, Philon allowed a couple of blow-bys off the dribble. He generally looked like he belonged on offense, albeit without any production in his brief run.

Maxey banked in a half-court heave at the first-quarter buzzer to put the Sixers up nine points. The Sixers couldn't carry forward any momentum, however, and began the second quarter poorly.

Adem Bona had another rough stint amid a subpar start to the season. After Anfernee Simons missed a transition layup try, Ryan Rollins' three lifted the Bucks into a 40-37 lead.

The dreadful stretch for the Sixers on both sides of the ball called to mind how they'd fallen into a 29-point deficit Thursday night vs. the Cavaliers before clawing out a comeback win.

The Sixers mustered just seven points in first six minutes of the second quarter and had many stagnant possessions that concluded with contested jumpers. The team's transition defense was dismal for much of the second period. Milwaukee had the game's first 19 fast-break points.

The Sixers regained the lead late in the second quarter. Kentavious Caldwell-Pope made two three-balls in the second and nabbed three first-half steals. Embiid assisted a go-ahead, and-one Walker layup.

Brown hit a three with 11.8 seconds left in the second quarter. Unsurprisingly, his variety of shotmaking skills were useful without James in the lineup.

Even when James or Embiid sit, the Sixers should have a simple advantage in terms of volume of stars over most opponents this year. None of Brown, Embiid or Maxey had the sort of off night that would have improved the Bucks' odds of a road win. They'd all passed the 20-point mark by the end of the third quarter.

Maxey notched another final-possession bucket, this time with a more conventional make. He canned a jumper from the right elbow with 1.7 seconds left in the third to extend the Sixers' lead to 97-87.

The Bucks made a late push in the fourth quarter. Kel'el Ware's put-back, and-one layup cut the Milwaukee's deficit to 117-114.

The Sixers ultimately handled business. Embiid reached his triple-double by assisting a second-chance Brown jumper and and Caldwell-Pope soon drilled a dagger corner three. Embiid even threw down a last-minute dunk for good measure.

For the second consecutive season, the Sixers have a 3-0 start. They got to four wins last year before dropping their first game.

#2661. Week 11 Fantasy Football Early Waiver Wire Pickups: Xavier Hutchinson, Antonio Williams among top options

We're approaching Week 11 of the 2026 fantasy football season and bye-pocalypse is nearly upon us. We have six teams on bye in Week 11 — the Packers, Rams, Seahawks, Patriots, Browns and Falcons. With so many teams off, you're likely going to have at least a hole or two in your lineup for a key matchup. We're here to help with some potential adds off the waiver wire.

The Houston passing game has really been clicking in two contests since the bye. Last week, we saw C.J. Stroud and Co. tear up the Chargers. In Week 10, the party continued (albeit in a stunning loss to the Browns) with Stroud tossing three TDs, one to Hutchinson, who now has a score in three straight games. He was second behind Nico Collins with four catches on seven targets for 58 yards and the TD, his third straight game reaching double-digit fantasy points.

There are going to be weeks in which the Texans spread it around, particularly once Marvin Harrison Jr. is back from injury. But the run game is non-existent for Houston, which should mean the team leans on the pass even more down the stretch. Hutchinson is playing the majority of snaps and is developing chemistry with Stroud. The wideout isn't a bad pickup if you need a spot start at WR or FLEX with Houston set to face the lowly Colts in Week 11.

Looking back to that TNF matchup between Washington and New York, Williams was a key contributor with two catches, one going for 31 yards and a TD. If we're chasing opportunity, Williams led Commanders WRs in snaps with 59 (86%) in the win. He finished with a 2-42-1 line for 11.2 fantasy points, and while we'd like to see Jayden Daniels give Williams more looks, that could be on the horizon. We hear the sentiment that rookies tend to improve in the second half and it's looking like Williams will be a priority in the passing game with Terry McLaurin out for the season.

Similar to Hutch, Williams is a decent WR or FLEX option with a potentially great game script in Week 11 against the Bengals. Williams has long-term value as well with solid matchups against the Cardinals, Titans and Texans after that.

We're all wide receivers in this edition, baby! Our third wideout recommendation is a player who will be coming off a bye in Denver's Bryant. He would have been a trendy pickup for Week 10 had the Broncos not been off, following a useful 4-56-1 line against the Panthers. Bryant has missed most of the 2026 season but when healthy, he's posted decent numbers with at least 6.2 fantasy points in four of five contests.

That isn't a huge figure but it's a decent floor for a player who may go overlooked on the wire this week. We also know that Jaylen Waddle sustained a concussion in Week 9. He should have ample time to get back for Week 11, but in the event Waddle is out, Bryant would get a nice boost. He's another target if you need a WR or FLEX option.

Alex Ovechkin's 22nd NHL season will be his last, the Washington Capitals superstar announced on Monday."This is gonna be my last year," Ovechkin told his teammates in a video the Capitals posted to social media. "It's sad, but it is what it is. We have an unbelievable team this year. There are 82 games left. Let's make the playoffs, and let's have fun."

Ovechkin has already established himself as the greatest goal-scorer in hockey history with 929 tallies, and he still has 82 games to add to that total before he hangs up his skates.

The No. 1 overall pick in the 2004 NHL Draft, Ovechkin immediately established himself as a prolific scorer by notching 52 goals en route to winning the Calder Trophy as a rookie.

Since then, Ovechkin has won the Rocket Richard Trophy as the NHL's leading goal-scorer a record nine times. The Capitals legend's resume also features an Art Ross Trophy and three Hart Trophy wins.

The crowning achievement in Ovechkin's illustrious career is leading Washington to its first Stanley Cup in 2017-18. After coming up short in a number of postseasons prior to that, Ovechkin led all playoff performers with 15 goals and won the Conn Smythe Trophy as a result.

Following the 2025-26 season, there was speculation that Ovechkin could retire, but he signed an incentive-laden one-year deal with the Caps.Sensing that this could be Ovechkin's final season, the Capitals loaded up to give their franchise icon one more shot at the Stanley Cup. Washington signed former Buffalo Sabres winger Alex Tuch in free agency and acquired winger Jordan Kyrou from the St. Louis Blues via trade.

No team is as loaded on the wings as the Capitals, and they have one of the best rosters in the Metro Division. Washington has the ingredients to challenge the defending Cup champion Carolina Hurricanes and get Ovechkin one more ring before he rides off into the sunset.

Dominick Barlow decided to finish his post-practice workout Saturday with a windmill dunk.

While Barlow remains out with a "lower back stress reaction" listing on the Sixers' injury report, it's one sign that he's trending up in his rehab process.

"He's making progress," Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said. "He was a part of the practice today. It's kind of a game day type of practice … so it wasn't super intense, as you might expect. But he was out there doing some stuff. He's progressing. Just don't know when he'll be ready to go, but at least he's making some progress now."

Barlow was one of the Sixers' top role players last season, starting 59 games and contributing in a variety of areas. He averaged 7.7 points, 4.8 rebounds, 1.2 assists and 0.9 steals in 23.8 minutes per game.

"Size, athleticism, rebounding," Dean Wade said of the fifth-year forward. "He's another guy that can switch one through five."

Whenever the 6-foot-9 Barlow is available for his season debut, the Sixers will welcome him back as another option at center.

With Ariel Hukporti's preseason Achilles tendon tear and Adem Bona's cervical spine sprain, the team is light on healthy resources at the five. He'll presumably return to the lineup when the Sixers visit the Nets on Monday night.

"I think (Barlow) is probably going to have to play more five than we envisioned," Nurse said, "but Jabari (Walker) is doing that as well. If the situation calls for that, I imagine that's where he'll help the most."

With the Delaware Blue Coats hosting the Maine Red Claws on Friday and Saturday, the Sixers saw an opportunity for two players outside of the regular rotation to log minutes with their G League affiliate.

Rookie guard Labaron Philon Jr. suited up Friday and third-year wing Justin Edwards played both games. Philon posted 20 points, nine rebounds and eight assists in a blowout loss. Edwards shot just 1 for 10 from the floor in the first game, but he scored 23 points on 9-for-17 shooting in Saturday's win.

Nurse has largely kept a tight rotation early in the season and the 10-3 Sixers haven't had many lopsided games with ample garbage time. As of Saturday night, the Sixers ranked 29th in the NBA in bench minutes per game.

"My first belief is it's hard to get better unless you're playing," Nurse said. "That kind of trumps everything, in my opinion. Just historically, we've had a number of guys that have gone down to those games, respected it … and it's really helped them in their careers. … It's been a minute for these guys — both of them — since they've had any real court time.

"So that fit into the schedule well. … I think it will also help them to just find some rhythm, find their legs a little bit. We're going to need everybody at some point, so keep 'em going."

VJ Edgecombe was among the crowd Friday night at Chase Fieldhouse.

#2657. Kirk Cousins gives Vikings what they expected. That's enough – for now

Even in a historically unique position for a quarterback, Kirk Cousins was exactly what the Minnesota Vikings literally bargained for.

In stepping in for Sunday's game against the Green Bay Packers after the Vikings acquired him Tuesday in a trade with the Las Vegas Raiders, the 15-year veteran became the first passer since at least 1950 to start for two different teams in consecutive weeks. Cousins, however, was no mystery box.

The 38-year-old isn't the same player he was when he departed the organization in 2024. But his value proposition as a pocket passer who can get through his progressions has long been evident, even if whatever team taking him on has had to endure a few hold-your-breath decisions in each game.

For a Vikings team that looked liable to waste a load-bearing defense, that familiar package – for all of its imperfections – was one the team would readily embrace.

Cousins' homecoming in a 30-10 win over the Packers fittingly featured few surprises, all in a mostly ideal fashion for a team both new and old to the quarterback.

And in completing 21 of 31 passes for 207 yards and two touchdowns, the signal-caller provided Minnesota with what it so sorely needed at midseason: a sense of timing and the possibility of sporadic escape from its problems.

The starkest contrast Cousins drew from Kyler Murray and Carson Wentz could be what he offered the offense once it fell in a hole.

Two of Cousins' best plays came on third-down strikes. On third-and-23 in the first quarter, he found Myles Price on a deep crosser, which the receiver then took into the end zone for a 38-yard score. That marked the longest third-down conversion throughout the NFL this season.

Cousins again delivered in another tough spot two drives later, when he lofted a third-and-15 pass down the left sideline that Tai Felton hauled in for a 24-yard gain. Aaron Jones plowed into the end zone for a 1-yard touchdown on the following play to put the Vikings up 17-0.

That kind of breakthrough might have felt transcendent to an attack accustomed to getting stuck in the mud. The Vikings entered the game tied for 30th in third-down conversion rate at 33.33%. On Sunday, they converted eight of 16 tries, including those two exceedingly difficult looks.

That's all part of the renewed sense of possibility with Cousins at the helm. Minnesota didn't pile up yards, but it played complementary football on a day when it won the turnover battle 4-1 and its defense generated eight sacks. And the offense kept churning in the fourth quarter, stringing together two long fourth-quarter scoring drives spanning more than 10 minutes to salt the game away.

"There's gonna be a lot of talk about offense and my addition here, but it's the defense," Cousins said in his postgame interview with Fox. "Our defense just played lights-out and kept giving us the ball back. I thought our staff did a great job of putting together a plan to allow me to be comfortable, and my teammates made plays and took it off my shoulders."

Cousins also quickly rekindled his connection with Justin Jefferson. The two-time All-Pro receiver notched a season-high nine catches for 74 receiving yards, making a particular dent on out-breaking routes.

Perhaps the most important element of Cousins' debut was the confidence he seemed to bring out of the rest of the operation. With the quarterback bringing back a sense of rhythm to the offense that had long been missing since his departure, the Vikings reclaimed access to the middle of the field. And coach Kevin O'Connell also did some of his best work in 2026 as a play-caller, showing particular creativity on the misdirection that left tight Gavin Bartholomew wide open for a 20-yard touchdown in the fourth quarter.

If Cousins is a known entity, so is his penchant for making the occasional cringeworthy decision.

That tendency bubbled to the surface again Sunday, as he heaved a regrettable interception to Packers safety Xavier McKinney toward the end of the first half, negating another possible scoring opportunity. He teetered on the verge of an even more calamitous decision earlier in the second quarter. Reviews showed Cousins' knee was down before he let go of a pass that would go on to be tipped and secured by edge rusher Lukas Van Ness.

And for all the progress the passing game displayed, the running game continued to get mostly middling results, netting 129 yards on 31 carries.

Cousins looked plenty comfortable in a game that conferred him plenty of advantages. Yet in a four-game losing streak with the Raiders, he had no answers for defenses that sent relentless waves of blitzes and man coverage. Packers defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon has ratcheted up his aggressiveness this season, but he didn't blitz on the two critical third-and-long conversions.

Can Cousins overcome his limitations against the NFC's elite? His initial showing is highly encouraging for the team's chances of navigating the NFC North, which is far and away the league's best division. But Minnesota has to have grander ambitions than just winning O'Connell's first playoff game. Cousins will have to figure out ways to counter the pressure of teams like the Seattle Seahawks, who can pick their spots in throwing extra rushers at the quarterback. And two weeks after his three-interception meltdown against the San Francisco 49ers, he'll get another chance at cracking Raheem Morris' defense in next Sunday's prime-time game in Mexico.

Still, after the Vikings broke out for their second-highest scoring output of the season – and biggest since the opener – it's easy to see why a team that so badly wanted to settle its quarterback question is finally feeling at ease. Even prior to the game, Ian Rapoport reported that the Vikings were interested in having Cousins back for 2027.

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Kirk Cousins gives Vikings what they expected. That's enough – for now

#2654. Four things to watch as Sixers look to respond against Raptors

Four things to watch as Sixers look to respond against Raptors originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers will not need to wait long for an opportunity to move past their most lopsided loss of the season.

Less than 48 hours after Boston's 123-101 win exposed several of Philadelphia's early weaknesses, the Sixers will host the Toronto Raptors on Thursday night at Xfinity Mobile Arena.

The Raptors are coming off a difficult meeting with the Celtics, too. Toronto led Boston by 22 points Wednesday before being outscored 61-34 over the final 29:24 of a 98-93 loss.

Philadelphia enters at 9-3 following Tuesday's defeat. Toronto is 5-6 and will complete a back-to-back and its third game in four nights.

LeBron James has been ruled out because of low-back and sciatica management. Joel Embiid is questionable with right plantar fascia injury management. Toronto will be without Kawhi Leonard, Scottie Barnes and Nate Bittle.

Here are four areas to watch as the Sixers try to respond.

Few teams have forced opponents into mistakes as frequently as Toronto.

The Raptors have generated 18.9 turnovers per game, the highest mark in the NBA. They are also averaging 10.9 steals and nearly 15 offensive rebounds.

The Sixers have countered that type of pressure well. Their 13.0 turnovers per game are tied for one of the lowest marks in the league.

Toronto's length remains disruptive even without Leonard and Barnes. The Raptors regularly crowd ball handlers, reach into passing lanes and send multiple players toward the offensive glass. Jakob Poeltl supplies size inside while RJ Barrett, Ja'Kobe Walter and Collin Murray-Boyles can create problems away from the ball.

The Raptors' pressure can punish a careless pass twice. It takes away a Sixers possession and gives Toronto an opportunity to score before the defense gets organized.

Philadelphia has largely avoided those mistakes while adjusting to a new lineup and playing at a quicker pace. Maintaining that control without James, who has handled a significant share of the playmaking, will be one of Thursday's clearest challenges.

Toronto has not built its offense around half-court shooting.

The Raptors are averaging 49.6 paint points and 16.4 fast-break points. Even while shorthanded Wednesday, they scored 18 points in transition against Boston.

That presents a direct test for a Sixers defense allowing 16.5 fast-break points per game, the fourth-highest figure in the NBA. Philadelphia has also surrendered 49.5 paint points per contest.

The first concern will be slowing the ball.

Immanuel Quickley returned Wednesday after missing two games with right hamstring soreness. He gives Toronto another guard capable of attacking early in the shot clock, while Barrett has consistently looked to get downhill with Leonard and Barnes unavailable.

Poeltl can create scoring chances without having a play called for him. He runs the floor, screens for Toronto's guards, rolls toward the rim and cleans up misses.

The Sixers have been effective in transition themselves, averaging 17.1 fast-break points. Maxey and VJ Edgecombe can change ends quickly after a stop, but Philadelphia must secure the ball first.

Thursday's game could swing on which team gets to run and which one is forced to create against a set defense.

Toronto provided an extreme example Wednesday of how quickly the three-point line can alter a game.

The Raptors entered their matchup against Boston shooting 31.8 percent from beyond the arc. They proceeded to hit 10 of their 18 attempts in the first quarter, tying a franchise record for threes in a period.

They went 6 for 25 over the final three quarters.

After Wednesday, Toronto is shooting 32.4 percent from three this season. The Sixers should not treat the Raptors like an elite perimeter team. They also cannot allow them to find early confidence through uncovered catch-and-shoot attempts.

Walter made five threes Wednesday and scored a team-high 17 points. Rookie Allen Graves added 13 points, while Quickley, Barrett and Jamison Battle are all willing shooters when the ball reaches them in rhythm.

Philadelphia's problems against Boston extended beyond the Celtics making difficult shots. The Sixers were late on several closeouts and occasionally allowed too much separation while navigating screens.

Toronto does not rely on the three as heavily as Boston. Wednesday showed it can still build a lead quickly when those shots start falling.

The Raptors expended significant energy Wednesday before traveling to Philadelphia.

They scored 38 first-quarter points, built a 22-point lead and then watched Boston erase the entire margin before the end of the third quarter. Quickley and Barrett each played more than 31 minutes. Poeltl and Walter both played at least 29.

The Sixers should have the fresher legs. Whether they take advantage could become apparent early.

Philadelphia has averaged 26.3 first-quarter points with a minus-2.2 scoring margin in opening periods. Slow starts have forced the Sixers to play from behind several times, including in their 29-point comeback against Cleveland.

An aggressive start would make Toronto respond quickly after a draining loss. Maxey and Edgecombe can apply pressure by pushing the ball after defensive rebounds instead of allowing the Raptors to set their pressure defense.

James' absence will require an adjustment. Maxey, Brown and Anfernee Simons should handle more of the ball and more of the decisions that come with initiating the offense.

If Embiid plays, the Sixers can make Toronto work through Poeltl by establishing him inside. If Embiid sits, Philadelphia's size concerns will become more pronounced with Adem Bona, Dominick Barlow and Ariel Hukporti also unavailable.

The Sixers have a rest advantage against a depleted opponent coming off an emotional loss. Their response should begin well before the fourth quarter.

#2650. Oliver Kahn fires back at Bayern over Musiala: "Loyalty is not a contractual obligation!"

Oliver Kahn has taken aim at Bayern Munich's handling of Jamal Musiala's health situation, delivering a strong message about loyalty, responsibility and player welfare. Following Uli Hoeneß's recent doubts about whether the 23-year-old can ever return to his previous level, the former Bayern CEO has offered a different perspective.

"Contractual loyalty is not loyalty. It is an obligation," Kahn wrote in a LinkedIn post. He argued that a club's true commitment only becomes apparent when a player can no longer deliver on the pitch.

"Clubs like to call themselves families. The problem starts when they talk about family as long as it costs nothing, and switch to talking numbers as soon as it becomes expensive," the 57-year-old added.

Kahn went even further, insisting that fulfilling a contract should not be celebrated as an extraordinary gesture of goodwill. "A club should not pretend that honouring the contract it signed itself is an act of particular humanity. The club did not just buy the performance. It also bought the risk."

The former goalkeeper also drew parallels with Manuel Neuer's serious leg injury in December 2022. Bayern publicly stood behind their captain before signing Yann Sommer just six weeks later.

"Both messages reach the player. But the second one is always heard much louder," Kahn concluded.

Musiala remains under contract until 2030, but has endured a difficult period with injuries and neurological issues. Bayern have stressed that continuing his playing career remains medically justifiable.

#2647. Fernando Mendoza's first NFL TD comes on designed run reminiscent of his iconic score that sealed Indiana's national championship

So far, so good for starting NFL quarterback Fernando Mendoza.

With Kirk Cousins playing and winning with the Minnesota Vikings on Sunday, the Mendoza era officially began in Las Vegas as the rookie quarterback made his first NFL start.

It began with reason for celebration on Las Vegas' first possession of the game against the reigning champion Seattle Seahawks.

Mendoza began his first NFL possession in good field position after a Seahawks fumble. He finished it 46 yards later with a 10-yard touchdown run for his first NFL score and a 7-0 Raiders lead.

Mendoza also completed all three of his first-possession passes for 20 yards before keeping the ball on a designed draw for the score.

The play was reminiscent of the touchdown Mendoza scored to cap Indiana's College Football Championship game win over Miami last season.

The Raiders used the No. 1 pick in the NFL Draft to select Mendoza after his Heisman Trophy-winning and national championship campaign. Save a brief appearance in a Week 5 loss to the Patriots, he spent his first eight NFL weeks learning from the bench with tutelage from Cousins.

But the Vikings traded for Cousins ahead of the trade deadline, starting the Mendoza era in earnest. And with the Super Bowl champions in town, Mendoza didn't blink on his first possession as an NFL starter.

#2646. Patrick Mahomes needed 1 real NFL WR to look like his scary self again

Even with a strong 7-2 record, something has felt off about the Kansas City Chiefs as they seek to regain AFC West supremacy this season. To be candid, that weird feeling has mostly been connected to Patrick Mahomes.

Entering Sunday's matchup with the Atlanta Falcons, the three-time Super Bowl MVP led a glorified checkdown-and-power-running offense. Per Sumer Sports, Mahomes' average depth of target was 5.74, good for 54th in the NFL. His average yards per pass attempt was just 7.7, which isn't necessarily bad, but it's notable that Mahomes hasn't surpassed eight yards per pass attempt since 2022, when he won his most recent regular-season MVP award.

If Sunday was the first Chiefs game you have watched all season, you wouldn't think Mahomes and Co. have had a problem throwing downfield at all. I guess that's what happens when you add a legitimate receiver like Josh Downs at the trade deadline to what is otherwise one of the NFL's most forgettable receiving depth charts. Mahomes was downright masterful against the Falcons, throwing five touchdown passes (with zero picks) for 348 yards with a 9.9 yards-per-pass-attempt average. Phew.

For all intents and purposes, he looked like his old self slinging deep bombs all over the field. That's scary news for the AFC's other Super Bowl contenders if Mahomes can keep this momentum going:

The Chiefs' lack of a consistent downfield element didn't and doesn't cost them against most NFL defenses, who don't have the horses to rally and tackle against well-coached offensive units. It does, however, become a major drawback against playoff-caliber defenses, as noted by Kansas City's road defeats to both the Seattle Seahawks and Denver Broncos. Against talented defenses, it's problematic when you can't keep them honest.

I'm not going to pretend the Chiefs have solved all of their passing issues after a single dominant win over an injury-riddled Falcons defense. We'll have to see Mahomes do this against defenses much better equipped to slow him and the Chiefs down over the second half of the season. Downs himself also isn't that kind of speedy receiver, even though he did catch four passes for 53 yards and a score. Nonetheless, it's a great sign for Kansas City that Mahomes can still unleash a deep ball with the best of them. His uncanny ability to create and throw backbreaking lasers has been what's separated the Chiefs from most everyone else during the Mahomes era.

All the Chiefs had to do to see this version of him resurface was find another legitimate boundary pass target.

You're telling me quarterbacks need solid receivers to throw the ball how they want? Huh. Who would have thought?

#2644. Observations after Sixers lose 1st Brown vs. Tatum matchup, George scores 36

Observations after Sixers lose 1st Brown vs. Tatum matchup, George scores 36 originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Round 1 of the new-look Sixers vs. the new-look Celtics decisively went Boston's way on Tuesday night.

In the first meeting between the teams since the July trade that sent Jaylen Brown to Philadelphia and Paul George to Boston, the Celtics earned a 123-101 win at Xfinity Mobile Arena.

The Sixers dropped to 9-3 and the Celtics improved to 9-2.

George was the game's brightest star, scoring 36 points on 14-for-22 shooting. Jayson Tatum added 21 points.

Tyrese Maxey's 24 points led the Sixers. Brown was hampered by foul trouble in his heavily anticipated first outing against Tatum. He posted 13 points, five rebounds and two assists in 26 minutes.

The Sixers will host the Raptors on Thursday night. Here are observations on their blowout loss to the Celtics:

To no one's surprise, Brown and Tatum guarded each other to open the night.

VJ Edgecombe defended a former teammate in George, who scored Boston's first four points with a pair of pure jumpers. On the other end, Maxey made the Sixers' first three field goals.

Judging by volume, the home fans cared most about the much-scrutinized Brown vs. Tatum matchup. The crowd was excited early when Brown snagged a steal and then dished to Maxey for a fast-break three-pointer. The fans also dialed up the noise when Brown sized up Tatum in isolation. He wound up dribbling the ball off his foot and out of bounds. Tatum pointed to signal it was Celtics ball.

Boston's star forward had a productive first quarter, posting 11 points. He scored an easy two when he used a back screen to break free from Brown and convert a layup that put the Celtics up 11-7. Boston began 9 for 12 from the floor as a team.

As for Brown, he sat shortly after being called for his second foul with 6:48 left in the first quarter.

Brown re-entered at the start of the second quarter. The Sixers still struggled to eat into Boston's lead.

A Sam Hauser triple extended the Celtics' advantage to 12 points. There was some audible frustration in the building after Brown missed two free throws on the next possesion.

The Sixers' deficit hit 16 points on a Hugo Gonzalez jumper. Meanwhile, the Sixers missed 12 of their first 14 three-point tries. While some of those shots were open looks that simply didn't go down, the Sixers also rushed up several contested jumpers before they made Boston's defense do serious work.

In the bigger picture, it wouldn't be remotely surprising if shooting stands out as a weak area for the Sixers come the trade deadline. They entered the game ranked 27th in the NBA in three-point frequency outside of garbage time and 22nd in three-point accuracy, according to Cleaning the Glass.

Joel Embiid (16 points, six rebounds) had an injury scare late in the second quarter when he fell hard after missing a layup in transition. He rose gingerly and limped through the final 30 seconds or so of the first half.

The Sixers' star big man was fine to start the third quarter and even drained a long-overdue three on the opening possession. He'd been in a terrible outside shooting slump (3 for 32 from deep on the season) before that shot.

Brown's foul trouble persisted. He picked up his fourth personal with 10:40 to go in the third quarter.

The Sixers stormed back without him and their defense played a large role. After LeBron James rumbled in for a layup, Dean Wade stonewalled Payton Pritchard on the perimeter to force a shot-clock violation. Wade later canned a three to even the contest at 76-all.

The Celtics responded and Tatum led the charge. His third-quarter exploits included a highlight slam on James and a top-of-the-key three to build Boston's lead back up to nine points.

Pritchard buried a three on the first possession of the fourth quarter and the Celtics' advantage kept growing. George celebrated a triple that stretched his team's lead to 100-82. The Sixers' spirits were considerably lower as they headed to their bench for a timeout. As a Sixer, George only had one higher-scoring game (39 points) than his performance Tuesday.

George and Tatum were each excellent in Philadelphia. Outside of Maxey, who finished 8 for 12 from the field, the Sixers didn't receive similar games from their stars.

Brown will be back in Boston on Jan. 21 when the Sixers visit the Celtics. He'll try to even the score.

#2642. Northville boys' soccer falls to Chazy in Class D state final

MIDDLETOWN - A minute after Chazy broke through in Sunday's Class D boys' soccer state final, Northville was down two goals.

Zeke McLennan scored in the 14th minute and Aidan Howell followed in the 15th as Section 7's Chazy went on to beat Northville 4-0 at Middletown High School to win its 11th state championship. Landon Duprey scored twice in the second half for Chazy, which finished 24-0.

Northville finished 20-2, with both losses coming against Chazy. The Eagles won the first meeting 2-1 in early October.

"Most people don't get to this point," Northville senior Niko Sevastakis said. "So I'm happy that we at least played the max amount of games we possibly could have - and I wouldn't want to do it with anyone else."

The Falcons entered Sunday with 17 shutout victories and a plus-141 goal differential. But getting through the previous two rounds took a comeback and a golden goal.

Northville trailed Edmeston Central 1-0 with seven minutes remaining in the regional final before Magnus Halloran tied it and McQuade Klippel scored the winner with 4:14 left. In Saturday's semifinal, Ryder Wright scored with seven minutes left in the first overtime to beat Section 11's Smithtown Christian 1-0.

Sunday marked Northville's second trip to the state final in three years. The Falcons beat Chazy 2-1 in overtime in the 2024 semifinals before losing to Hamilton in the final. Chazy ended Northville's season in the regional final last fall.

When Northville reached the state semifinals two years ago, the players bleached their hair. This time, they got buzz cuts. Sevastakis said it was a way to bond with teammates he called "a big family."

"I learned a lot of things beyond soccer, being on this team," Sevastakis said.

Northville coach Steve Clapper said one of the most rewarding parts of this year's run was watching the community rally around his players.

"The community support has just been incredible," Clapper said. "I think it's really amazing to see the community come together and really support these guys who deserve that."

With a group of underclassmen set to return next season, Clapper expects the experience to give them more reason to push for another trip to Middletown.

"We'll be back here again," he said. "No doubt."

#2640. Observations after Sixers shake off slow start, Embiid injury scare to win

Observations after Sixers shake off slow start, Embiid injury scare to win originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers brushed off their blowout loss to the Celtics and got back in the win column Thursday night.

They overcame a first-quarter deficit as high as 17 points and earned a 123-112 home win over the Raptors. The Sixers moved to 10-3 and Toronto fell to 5-7.

Tyrese Maxey had 27 points and eight assists. Joel Embiid added 20 points.

Jaylen Brown tallied 18 points and six rebounds. VJ Edgecombe posted 15 points, eight rebounds and a season-high eight assists. Anfernee Simons scored 17 points and shot 5 for 6 from three-point range.

RJ Barrett recorded 31 points and 14 rebounds. Immanuel Quickley had 26 points and six assists.

The Sixers were without LeBron James (low back/sciatica management), Adem Bona (cervical spine sprain), Dominick Barlow (lower back stress reaction) and Ariel Hukporti (right Achilles tendon tear).

The team told reporters Thursday morning that Bona will be re-evaluated in approximately one week and that Barlow participated in shootaround. The 23-year-old forward also went through a pregame workout on the Xfinity Mobile Arena floor. There's no formal timetable for his return.

Toronto's sidelined players included Kawhi Leonard and Scottie Barnes.

The Sixers will face the Pacers on Sunday afternoon in Philadelphia. Here are observations on their victory over the Raptors:

Dean Wade began the game in James' normal spot. The Sixers started slowly, missing their first foul field goals and opening 1 for 8 from three-point range.

He stayed down after setting a ball screen and having an apparent knee-to-knee collision with Ja'Kobe Walter. The Sixers called timeout with 8:30 left in the first quarter and Embiid grabbed at his right knee. He eventually rose with assistance from teammates and Sixers head athletic trainer Kevin Johnson, then limped back to the locker room. Jabari Walker entered.

At the 5:26 mark of the first quarter, Embiid checked back in to cheers from the home fans.

"I knew that he didn't twist it or anything," Maxey said. "I knew it was a knee-to-knee, so I wasn't too worried. He kept saying, 'I just got kneed.' That still hurts, though."

Embiid ended up logging 28 minutes, though he certainly wanted to play more.

"He was very, very motivated to play," Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said. "It was hard to get him out for his scheduled rests tonight, which is a good problem sometimes."

While Embiid's return was a major positive development, the Sixers fell further behind. The Raptors' lead swelled to 32-16 with a Jamison Battle three-pointer and Nurse burned a timeout.

Simons sunk a buzzer-beating three to conclude the first quarter, cutting the Sixers' deficit to nine points.

"Those are big momentum plays that usually have some weight to them and carry you into the next moment," Nurse said.

The Sixers kept rolling against a shorthanded Toronto team playing on the second night of a back-to-back. Simons nailed a triple to kick off the scoring in the second quarter. Brown buried a mid-range jumper and Edgecombe jammed in a crowd-pleasing dunk to give the Sixers a 35-34 edge.

Brown and Edgecombe shined in the second quarter both as individuals and as a duo. The Sixers need Edgecombe to attack a bit more offensively when he shares the floor with Brown and bench players. It doesn't hurt for the second-year guard to have that clarity about his role in those units.

"He's one of our better playmakers," Maxey said of Edgecombe. "He's really good at getting downhill and creating for himself and others."

The Sixers' only three bench rotation players were Walker, Simons and Kentavious Caldwell-Pope (11 points, five assists). In addition to Walker, Wade got center minutes behind Embiid.

Embiid picked up his third foul with 2:23 left in the second quarter and had to take a seat. The teams were tied at 60 apiece through two periods.

The game remained even for much of the third, but Maxey fueled an 11-0 Sixers run late in the quarter.

His speed and the Sixers' collective focus on pushing the pace whenever possible allowed the team to get regular points before Toronto could set its defense. Maxey zoomed in for a layup, then tossed the ball ahead to Brown for an easy bucket. Brown assisted a Simons three. Walker converted a fast-break lay-in and canned a three on the first possession of the fourth quarter. All of a sudden, the Sixers held a 101-87 lead.

Brown, Edgecombe and the bench gave the Sixers more good minutes early in the fourth quarter. They sealed the deal without any late drama. And the fans chanting for a Tacko Fall appearance got their wish with a final-minute entrance by the 7-foot-6 center.

#2636. Rangers lose star goaltender Igor Shesterkin for season with lower-body injury; what's next for New York?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Rangers goaltender Igor Shesterkin will miss the remainder of the season with a lower-body injury, the team announced on Saturday.

Shesterkin suffered an apparent leg injury in the Rangers' loss to the Washington Capitals on Friday night as his right leg slid awkwardly into the post while scrambling to get back in position. Shesterkin fell to the ice immediately, and he needed assistance to get down the tunnel.

Prior to that loss, the Rangers were off to a terrific 4-1-0 start, and Shesterkin was a driving force behind that success. In just five appearances, Shesterkin posted 3.90 goals saved above average with a .900 high-danger save percentage, according to Natural Stat Trick.

The 2022 Vezina Trophy winner, Shesterkin has put up sparkling numbers since he entered the NHL in 2019-20. In 330 games, Shesterkin boasts a .917 save percentage, a 2.51 GAA and 22 shutouts. Over the last three full seasons from 2023-26, Shesterkin ranked third in goals saved above average with 45.4. Only Connor Hellebuyck and Andrei Vasilevskiy were better in that category.

Shesterkin was a big reason why the Rangers felt they could bounce back from a disappointing 2025-26 season, and losing the star goaltender puts a huge dent in the team's playoff hopes. It doesn't help that backup goalie Joonas Korpisalo is also hurt.

Dylan Garand replaced Shesterkin on Friday night, and Spencer Martin will be recalled from the AHL after recovering from his own injury. With the Rangers playing well early, it wouldn't be a shock to see them explore better replacement options for Shesterkin.

New York won't be able to replace Shesterkin's impact because he's one of the five best goalies in the world. However, the team should be able to upgrade its current goaltending situation, which is a fairly low bar to clear.

First, there are unsigned veterans still on the open market in Petr Mrazek and James Reimer. Neither one was great last season -- hence their availability at the moment -- Reimer and Mrazek could provide a level of stability in the crease that the Rangers simply don't have right now.

New York could also explore trade possibilities, and Minnesota Wild netminder Filip Gustavsson could be a solution there. Jesper Wallstedt is the future of the crease in Minnesota, making Gustavsson more of a luxury. Would the Wild send Gustavsson to New York in exchange for some draft capital it could use to acquire a center?

The one snag in a potential Gustavsson deal is his contract. Gustavsson is in the first year of a deal that pays him $6.8 million over the next five seasons. That's a big commitment for a player who will become a backup when Shesterkin returns.

Obviously, Connor Hellebuyck has been on the trade market for months now, but that trade wouldn't make sense for the Rangers. Hellebuyck is on an expensive long-term deal, and New York would have $20 million tied up in goalies if they made that move, not to mention the astronomical acquisition cost.

However, if you'll allow me to get creative here, it's no secret that the Florida Panthers have pursed Hellebuyck. What if the Panthers traded Jacob Markstrom -- just acquired in the offseason -- to the Rangers in order to make room for Hellebuyck?

Markstrom does have a 20-team no-trade list, so the question is whether New York would be one of his 11 approved teams. Florida flipping Markstrom so quickly seems like a long shot, but the team has taken plenty of big swings in recent history.

#2634. England beat Spain in Nations League to end record unbeaten run

England snapped world champions Spain's record unbeaten run with a 3-2 victory in Madrid on Sunday to clinch the top spot in Nations League group A3.

Goals from Harry Kane, Ezri Konsa and Ben White inflicted La Roja's first loss in a competitive game since March 2023, after 44 without defeat.

England's Elliot Anderson was sent off in the second half as Spain fought back from three goals down with strikes from Mikel Oyarzabal and Nico Williams, but Luis de la Fuente's World Cup winners could not find the equaliser.

Both sides were already sure to progress, but as group winners England will be seeded for the quarter-finals in March.

Spain had beaten England in the Euro 2024 final before adding a second world crown this summer, while the Three Lions finished third.

"We knew we were going to beat them tonight, the message from the manager after the Croatia game (on Thursday) has been so positive," England midfielder Declan Rice told ITV.

"The first 10 minutes was the best we've played."

England coach Thomas Tuchel hailed his team on their superb performance in the Spanish capital.

"We brought everything to the table," Tuchel told ITV.

"We were brave. Spirit wise, energy wise and also football quality was (all at the) highest level."

Tuchel selected James Trafford in goal over Jordan Pickford and also brought White and Konsa into the side.

Teenage star Lamine Yamal was fit to start for Spain at Atletico Madrid's Metropolitano stadium after missing their midweek win over the Czech Republic.

However the youngster did not see much of the ball in the first half as England came out strongly.

Spain goalkeeper Unai Simon produced a strong reaction save to deny Jude Bellingham, while Anthony Gordon had a dangerous shot blocked.

Ballon d'Or winner Kane, who beat Yamal to the award, sent an effort narrowly wide.

Barcelona defender Pau Cubarsi handed England the advantage when he clumsily felled Kane in the area on the stroke of half time.

The Bayern Munich hitman powered a perfect penalty past Simon, who dived the right way but to no avail.

De la Fuente tried to react at half-time with a triple change, including throwing on Barcelona duo Fermin Lopez and Pedri, but England quickly found more joy.

Konsa headed home the second from Declan Rice's corner in the 53rd minute after the Arsenal defender was left unmarked by Spain's defence.

Four minutes later England sliced open Spain's defence with Kane and Bellingham combining to set up White for the third.

La Roja clawed their way back into the game when Anderson fouled Yamal in the area as the Spain striker ran in on goal.

The Manchester City midfielder was dismissed and Oyarzabal slotted home the penalty.

Spain found a second when Gordon gave the ball away and Yamal fed Williams, whose shot hit the post and bounced in.

Williams curled over and Trafford superbly denied Yamal and Marc Cucurella as Spain looked fruitlessly for the goal they needed to preserve their unbeaten record.

Including friendlies, Spain had gone 43 straight matches without defeat.

"On the pitch everything happens very fast, it's a pity," Oyarzabal told TVE about England's two goals early in the second half.

"You have to focus on what came after, the reaction -- the team never stopped pushing, never stopped trying... their goalkeeper also deserves credit for us not having equalised."
